s: 2 Corinthians 1:14 — You have already recognized, at least in part, that we are your joy, just as you also are our joy on the day of the Lord Jesus.
Earlier in this chapter, the apostle Paul tells about the great troubles he faced while serving as a minister.
In our text and the two verses before it, he tells what comforted him and held him up during those troubles.
He names four things in particular.

1. First, his own conscience approved of him. He says in verse 12: “This is what makes us glad: our conscience tells us that we have lived in the world with simple honesty and a sincerity that comes from God. We did not rely on worldly wisdom but on God’s grace. And we lived this way even more toward you.”

2. The second comfort he mentions is this. His own conscience approved of him, and so did the consciences of his listeners, the Corinthians he was now writing to. And they would approve of him on the day of judgment.
3. Third, he hoped to see the good fruit of all his work and suffering as a minister. He would see it in their happiness and glory on that great day when everyone must give an account.
4. Fourth, in his work among the Corinthians, he had been approved by his Judge. And that Judge would approve and reward his faithfulness on that day.

The last three of these are shown in my text and the verse before it. In fact, all four are hinted at in the text. The text suggests that the Corinthians had accepted Paul as their spiritual father. They saw him as someone who had been faithful among them. He was the one God used to bring them their future joy and glory on the day of judgment. They would see him then and have a joyful meeting with him. The text also suggests that Paul expected to have a joyful meeting with them at that time, standing before the Judge. He expected to see their glory with joy, because it was the fruit of his work. In that way they would be his joy. The text also suggests that he expected the great Judge to approve of him when he and they met together before him. The Judge would then recognize that Paul had been faithful, and that this faithfulness had helped bring them to glory. And so the Judge would, in a way, give them to Paul as his crown of joy.
But Paul could not hope for any of this unless his own conscience was on his side.
So these words show very strongly that his own conscience approved of him.
There is one thing hidden in each of these points, and in every part of the text. That is the point I will make the subject of my sermon today. Here it is:
Ministers and the people in their care will have to meet each other before Christ’s judgment seat on the day of judgment.

Ministers and the people who have been in their care must be parted in this world, no matter how close they have been. If nothing separates them sooner, death will part them. And they may be separated even while they are still alive.

We live in a world of change. Nothing here is certain or steady. In a short time, in just a few years, strange things happen. Surprising changes come to people, to families, to towns and churches, and to countries and nations.
It often happens that people who seem the closest are soon the most divided and the farthest apart.

So it is with ministers and their people. They may have had the greatest respect for each other and the closest bond. Yet they may come to disagree in their opinions and grow cold in their feelings. One side may even break away from the other, and the whole relationship may be ended. The minister may be moved to a faraway place. They may never have anything to do with each other again in this world.
But even if that happens, there is one more meeting they must have. That meeting will be on the last great day, when everyone must give an account.
Here I want to show three things:
I. How ministers and the people who have been in their care will meet each other on the day of judgment.
II. Why they will meet.
III. Why God has arranged for ministers and their people to meet together then, in this way and for these purposes.
I. First, I want to show in a few points how ministers and the people who have been in their care will meet each other on the day of judgment.
About this I want to point out two general things.
1. They will not just meet the way all people will meet then. There will be something special about the way they meet.
2. Their meeting at that time will be very different from the way they used to meet in God’s house in this world.
1. On that day they will not meet the way the whole world will meet together.
I want to point out two differences.
(1) The first difference is that they will clearly see each other. They will know and notice each other distinctly.

The whole world will be there on that day. All people from every generation will be gathered in one huge crowd, along with all the angels, both the chosen angels and the fallen ones. But we don’t need to think that everyone will know every single person in that whole crowd. There will surely be many millions upon millions of them.
People will probably be able to understand far more then than they can now. But their minds will not be unlimited. Their understanding will grow enormously, but people will not become gods.

Each person will probably be able to see much of that huge crowd and much of what happens on that great day. But minds that have limits can only take in so much. So on that day, each person will notice some people and some things more than others. And we can guess that this will depend on who they were most connected with in what happens that day.

There is a special reason why people who had special dealings with each other in this world will be placed where they can see each other. This life was their time of testing. On that day, their dealings with each other will be examined and judged.

So we can expect that rulers and the people they ruled, earthly judges and the people they judged, and neighbors who talked, did business, and argued with each other will meet then. So will the heads of families and their children and servants. They will be placed together in a special way.

This will be true most of all for ministers and their people. Our text makes it clear that they will see each other. They will know each other clearly and pay special attention to each other at that time.
(2) The second difference is that they will meet as people who have special business with each other in the great events of that day.
They will meet the whole world at that time. But they will not have direct, personal business with everyone.
In fact, most of the people gathered there will be people they never had anything to do with during their time of testing on earth. So they will have nothing between them to be judged.

But ministers and the people who have been in their care are different. They have had a great deal to do with each other directly. And it was about the most important matters that people can ever share with one another.
So they especially must meet and be brought together before the Judge. They have special business with each other in the purpose and work of that great day when everyone gives an account.
So the way they meet will be different from the way people in general meet.
2. Their meeting on the day of judgment will be very different from the ways they meet with each other in this world.
While the relationship lasts, ministers and their people often meet together in this world.
They usually meet every Sunday, and at other times too. They come together for public worship, to share in the sacraments, and for the serious services of God’s house.

Besides these meetings, they also meet at times to decide and run the business of the church. They meet to carry out church discipline. And they meet to settle matters that keep the church’s public worship pure and in good order.
But their meeting on the day of judgment will be extremely different from any meeting they have with each other now, both in how it happens and in what surrounds it.
Let me show how, in a few points.
(1) Now they meet at a time of preparation, when things can still change. But then they will meet when nothing can change anymore.

Now sinners in the church meet their minister at a time when they can still be changed and saved. Through God’s blessing on the pastor’s preaching and work, they can still be turned from Satan’s power to God. They can be brought out of guilt, condemnation, and God’s anger. They can be brought into peace and friendship with God. They can enjoy the privileges of his children and have a right to their eternal inheritance.

And true believers now meet their minister while much sin still remains in them. Sometimes they are struggling with great spiritual problems and pain. So they can still be helped to reach a happier condition, with more freedom from these things. They have reason to hope for this help as they faithfully take part in worship and the sacraments. And God usually chooses to use his ministers to bring this help.
Ministers and their people meet now to bring about these happy changes. These are the great blessings they look for when they meet for worship in this world.
But when they meet together on the day of judgment, it will be very different.
They will not meet then to use the means God gives to bring about any such changes. That is because they will all be in a state that can never change.

Sinners will not be able to change. Those who are still guilty and ruled by sin then, with God’s anger resting on them, will be past all help. There will be no chance of change for them. They will meet their ministers with no hope of relief or rescue, and no hope of getting any good from them.

And the true believers will already be completely free from all the sin, temptation, and troubles of every kind that still clung to them before. They will be placed forever out of reach of those things. There will be no more rescue or happy change left to happen through the means of grace or the work of ministers.
Then it will be announced: “Let the unjust stay unjust, and the filthy stay filthy. Let the righteous stay righteous, and the holy stay holy.”
(2) Then they will meet together in a light that is clear, certain, and free from any mistake.

Ministers are placed in the church as guides and teachers. The Bible pictures them as lights set up in the churches. In this life they meet their people again and again to teach them and help them understand. They correct their mistakes. When the people turn aside to the right or to the left, the minister is like a voice behind them saying, “This is the way. Walk in it.” Ministers prove and support the truth by showing the evidence for it. They answer errors and false ideas. They try to convince those who are wrong and to make those who doubt more sure.

But when Christ comes to judge, every error and false idea will be exposed. All lies and illusions will disappear in the light of that day, the way the darkness of night disappears when the sun rises. Every teaching of God’s word will then be plainly shown to be true, and no one will remain unconvinced. Everyone will know the truth with complete certainty, and there will be no mistakes left to correct.

Now ministers and their people may disagree about some matters of faith. Sometimes they meet to talk about the things they disagree on and to hear the reasons given by each side. But all of it may fail to convince anyone of the truth. They may meet and part again, agreeing no more than before. The side that was wrong may stay wrong. Sometimes, when ministers and people disagree like this, their meetings turn into unhappy arguments and fights. People argue with a lot of prejudice and without being fair or open. Instead of bringing light and helping people see the truth, these meetings make the darkness deeper and stronger. They harden people against the truth and push them further apart from each other.

But later, when they meet together on the day of judgment before the great Judge’s throne, the mind and will of Christ will be made known. There will be no more arguments or differences of opinion. The truth will be so clear that no one can dispute it. Every disagreement will be settled once and for all, forever.

Now ministers meet their people to open the eyes of sinners’ consciences and wake them up. They show sinners how evil and dangerous sin is. They show them how strict God’s law is and how wicked their own hearts and actions are. They show them how guilty they are and that God’s anger rests on them. They show them that they are powerless, blind, poor, helpless, and lost. But often all this does no good. No matter what their ministers say, they stay numb and asleep, and their consciences are not convinced.

But it will not be like that at their last meeting on the day of judgment. When sinners meet their minister before their great Judge, their conscience will not be numb. They will be fully convinced that the things they heard from him were true. They will know the greatness and terrifying majesty of God. They will know his holiness, his hatred of sin, and his fearful justice in punishing it. They will know how strict his law is and how true and dreadful his warnings are. They will know their own guilt and misery, which are too great for words. And they will never again be able to ignore these things. The eyes of their conscience will then be fully opened and will never be blinded again. The mouth of their conscience will be opened and will never be shut again.

Now ministers meet with their people, in public and in private, to help them understand the condition of their souls. They explain the rules of God’s word and apply them to the people, so that they will search their own hearts and see what condition they are in.
But ministers today cannot see perfectly into the souls of their own people. Even the wisest of them can make mistakes, and they often are wrong about these things.

The people also cannot know for sure what condition their minister is in, or what condition each other is in. Very often people are thought of as true believers, maybe even as outstanding believers, when they are really terrible hypocrites. On the other hand, some people are criticized, or barely accepted by others, when they are really some of God’s precious jewels.

And nothing is more common than for people to be wrong about their own condition. Many people whom God finds detestable, and who are under his anger, think very highly of themselves. They believe they are his precious saints and dear children.

In fact, there is reason to think this: some people are very bold in feeling sure that they are safe and happy. They think they are not only true believers but the most outstanding believers in the church. Yet often these very people are, in a special way, like smoke in God’s nose.

And this surely happens often, even in churches where God’s word is preached most faithfully. It happens no matter how clearly ministers explain God’s teachings and rules, and no matter how deeply they apply them to their listeners’ souls when they meet together.

But on the day of judgment they will have a different kind of meeting. Then the secrets of every heart will be brought into the open, and everyone’s true condition will be completely known. Look at 1 Corinthians 4,

verse 5: “So don’t judge anything too soon, before the Lord comes. He will bring into the light what is hidden in darkness, and he will show what people’s hearts were planning. Then each person will receive praise from God.”
Then no one will be fooled about his own condition, and no one will be unsure about it anymore.
All the false pride and empty hopes of fooled hypocrites will end forever. So will all the doubts and fears of sincere Christians.

And then everyone will know the condition of each other’s souls. The people will know whether their minister was sincere and faithful. The ministers will know the condition of every one of their people. They will know for whom God’s word and sacraments were a sweet smell that leads to life, and for whom they were a smell that leads to death.

In this life, when ministers and people meet to discuss and run church business, especially when there is a conflict, they are quick to judge and criticize each other. They judge each other’s opinions and plans, and the motives and goals behind what each one does. They are often badly mistaken in their judgments, and they treat each other unfairly with their criticism.

But at that future meeting, everything will be shown in a true and perfect light. The motives and goals behind everything each person did will be known for certain. There will be an end to all mistakes like these and to all unfair criticism.

(3) In this world, ministers and their people often meet to hear about a Lord they cannot see and to serve him. But on the day of judgment, they will meet right in front of him, where they can see him.

Now ministers often meet their people to preach to them about the King who is eternal, who never dies, and who cannot be seen. They try to convince them that there is a God and tell them what he is like. They try to convince them that he rules the world and will judge it, and that there will be rewards and punishments after this life. They preach to them about Christ, who is in heaven at God’s right hand in a world we cannot see. But then these ministers will meet their people face to face with this great God, Savior, and Judge. He will appear in the plainest, most visible, and most open way, with great glory and with all his holy angels, before them and the whole world.

They will not meet to hear about a Christ who is absent, a Lord who is unseen, and a Judge who is still to come. They will meet to stand before that Judge. They will be placed together in the presence of that supreme Lord, in his enormous glory and awesome majesty. He is the one they heard about so often when they met together on earth.
(4) On the last day, when ministers meet the people who have been in their care, no one will come with a careless, unthinking heart.

But many people come to church meetings in this world with just that kind of heart. They pay little attention to the God they claim to worship together in the serious duties of public worship. They pay little attention to their own thoughts or the state of their minds. They don’t focus on what they are doing or think about why they have come together.

But the meeting on that great day will be very different. There will not be one careless heart. No one will be sleeping. No one’s mind will wander from the great business of that meeting. No one will be inattentive to what is happening that day. No one will ignore whose presence they are in. No one will ignore the great things they will hear from Christ at that meeting. Nor will they ignore what they heard from him and about him through their ministers back when they met during their time of testing. Nor will they ignore what they will then hear their ministers say about them before their Judge.

I have now pointed out these things about how this future meeting will happen, when ministers and the people in their care stand before Christ’s judgment seat on the day of judgment. Now I will move on.
II. Next, I want to show why they will meet then.
1. They will meet to give an account to the great Judge of how they treated each other in the relationship they had in this world.

Christ sends ministers to their people to do his work. They are his servants and messengers. When they have finished their service, they must go back to their master and report to him. They must tell him what they did and how they were received while doing their work.
We see this in Luke 14,

verses 16–21. A servant was sent out to invite guests to a great dinner. When he had done his job and finished the work he was given, he went back to his master. He reported what he had done and how he had been received.
Then the master grew angry and sent his servant out to other people. And again the servant came back and told his master what he had done and how it had gone.
We also read in Hebrews 13,
verse 17, that ministers are leaders in God’s house, “who keep watch over souls, as people who will have to give an account.”

And we see from that passage in Luke 14 that ministers must report to their master about more than their own behavior in their work. They must also report how their people received them and how they were treated by them.
They will be called to report on both of these things. So they will give their report on that great day of accounts in front of their people. Both they and their people will stand before their Judge.
Faithful ministers will then report with joy about those who welcomed them and made good use of their ministry. On that day, those people will be given to them as their crown of joy.

At the same time, they will report how badly they were treated by those who did not welcome them or the messages they brought from Christ. They will not meet these people the way they used to in this world, to give them advice and warnings. Instead, they will testify against them. They will sit with Christ as their judges and as his helpers in the court, to condemn them.

On the other hand, on that day the people will stand up in the judgment against wicked and unfaithful ministers. Those ministers cared more about their own earthly gain than about the good of the souls in their flock.

2. At that time, ministers and the people who have been in their care will meet together before Christ so that he can judge between them. He will settle any disputes they had with each other in this world.
In this evil world, it very often happens that big disagreements and disputes come up between ministers and the people in their care.

They have a greater duty to live in peace than people in almost any other relationship. And for many reasons, fights and divisions between people in this kind of relationship have the saddest and most terrible results of any kind of conflict. Yet how often such fights have happened!

Sometimes a church fights with its minister about his teaching. Sometimes they fight about how he leads and behaves. And sometimes they fight about his pay. Sometimes these fights go on for a long time. Sometimes they are settled in this world by whichever side has more power, instead of by God’s word and what is reasonable. And sometimes these disputes are never properly settled in this world at all.
But on the day of judgment, they will be decided fully, perfectly, and forever.

The Judge who never makes mistakes, the endless source of light, truth, and justice, will judge between the two sides. He will declare what is true, who is right, and what agrees with his mind and will.

That is why both sides must stand together before him on the last day. That will be the great day for ending and settling every dispute. It will be the day for correcting every mistake and doing away with every unfair judgment, error, and confusion that has ever existed among people.

3. Ministers and the people who have been in their care must meet together at that time to receive an eternal sentence from the Judge and get what they deserve. They will receive it in front of each other, based on how they behaved toward each other in the relationship they had in this life.
The Judge will not only say what is just. He will also carry out justice between ministers and their people.

He will declare what is right between them. He will approve the one who has been fair and faithful and condemn the one who has not. His sentence will be perfectly true and fair, and so will the rewards he gives and the punishments he hands out.
Faithful ministers will receive a glorious reward. This includes those whose work bore fruit, as Daniel 12,

verse 3 says: “Those who are wise will shine as bright as the sky. Those who lead many people to do what is right will shine like the stars forever and ever.” It also includes those who were faithful but did not see results, as Isaiah 49,
verse 4 says: “Then I said, ‘My work has been useless. I have used up my strength for nothing. Yet the Lord will surely judge my cause, and my reward is with my God.’”
And those who welcomed and received them well will be gloriously rewarded, as Matthew 10,
verses 40 and 41 say: “Whoever takes you in takes me in. And whoever takes me in takes in the one who sent me.
Whoever takes in a prophet because he is a prophet will get a prophet’s reward. And whoever takes in a righteous man because he is righteous will get a righteous man’s reward.”
Such people and their faithful ministers will be each other’s crown of joy, as 1 Thessalonians 2,
verses 19 and 20 say: “What is our hope, our joy, our crown of joy?
Isn’t it you, standing before our Lord Jesus Christ when he comes?
Because you are our glory and our joy.”
Our text says the same thing: we are your joy, just as you are ours, on the day of the Lord Jesus.
But those who mistreat Christ’s faithful ministers, especially for the very things in which they are faithful, will be severely punished, as Matthew 10,
verses 14 and 15 say: “If anyone will not receive you or listen to what you say, shake the dust off your feet when you leave that house or city.
This is the truth: on the day of judgment, things will go easier for the sinners of Sodom and Gomorrah than for that city.”
Deuteronomy 33:8–11 says: “About Levi he said, ‘Let your Urim and Thummim belong to your holy one....
They will teach your rules to Jacob and your law to Israel....
Lord, bless all he owns, and accept the work of his hands. Break the strength of those who stand up against him and of those who hate him, so that they never get up again.’”
On the other hand, ministers who turn out to have been unfaithful will suffer a most terrible punishment.
See Ezekiel 33:6 and Matthew 23:1–33.
So on that great day, justice will be done to ministers and their people.

That is why they will meet together. They will not only receive justice themselves, but also see justice done to the other side. This is the whole purpose of that great day: to show and declare God’s righteous judgment, as Romans 2,
verse 5 says. Ministers will receive justice, and they will see justice done to their people. And the people will receive justice and see justice done to their minister.

In this way, everything between them will be set right and settled forever. Each person will be sentenced and paid back according to what he has done. Some will receive and wear a crown of eternal joy and glory. Others will suffer shame and pain that never ends.
Now I come to the next thing I promised to show, which is this:
III. I want to give some reasons why we can believe God has arranged for ministers and the people in their care to meet together on the day of judgment, in this way and for these purposes.
There are two things I want to point out now:
1. What goes on between ministers and their people is extremely important.

The Bible says that God will bring every deed into judgment, including every secret thing, whether it is good or evil. It is right that everything people are involved in and everything they do, in public and in private, should finally be brought before God’s judgment seat. There a Judge who never makes mistakes will settle it once and for all. But this is especially needed for matters that are very important.
And what goes on between a Christian minister and his church is enormously important. In many ways it matters much more than the earthly concerns of the greatest kings and their kingdoms or empires.

It matters enormously how ministers do their job, and how they behave toward their people in their work and in everything connected with it. It also matters enormously how a church receives and treats a faithful minister of Christ, and what use they make of his ministry.

These things are more closely and directly connected to the great, final purpose God made people for, and to their eternal well-being, than any of people’s earthly concerns, whether public or private.

So it is especially right that these matters should be brought into judgment and openly decided and settled with truth and fairness. And for this reason, ministers and their people should meet together before the Judge who knows everything and never makes mistakes.
2. What goes on between ministers and their people is closely connected to the main things that will happen on the day of judgment.
It is closely connected to the great and divine person who will appear as Judge on that day.

Ministers are his messengers, sent out by him. In their work among their people, they represent him and stand in his place. They are sent to tell what he thinks, to do his work, and to speak and act in his name.
So it is especially right that they should go back to him and report on their work and how it turned out.
A king is the judge of all the people in his kingdom. They must all answer to him.

But it is even more important for the king’s officials to come back and report to him. They are the ones especially trusted to run his kingdom, and they are sent out on special missions. They must report on themselves, on how they carried out what they were trusted with, and on how they were received.

Ministers are not only messengers of the one who will appear as Judge on the last day. The mission they are sent on, and the business he has trusted them with as his servants, directly affects his honor and the good of his kingdom.

Their work is to move forward the plans of his rule and government. So their work with their people is closely connected to the day of judgment. The great purpose of that day is to completely settle and establish the business of his kingdom. On that day everything that has to do with it will be set right. Everything that works against his kingdom will be removed. Everything that helps make it complete and glorious will be made perfect and firm. And so this great King will receive the honor and glory he deserves.

Again, what goes on between ministers and their people is directly connected to what happens on the day of judgment. Ministers work with their people to help people’s souls be saved forever and escape eternal damnation. And the day of judgment is the day set for that very purpose. On that day, where people will spend eternity will be openly decided and settled. Some will be fixed forever in salvation, and their salvation will be brought to its fullest completion. Others will be fixed forever in damnation and the deepest misery.
What goes on between ministers and people is most directly connected to the day of judgment, because the whole purpose of a minister’s work is to get people ready for that day.

Ministers are sent to warn people that the day is coming. They warn them ahead of time about the terrible sentence that will be announced against the wicked. They tell them about the blessed sentence that will be announced for the righteous. And they use every means with them, so that they can escape the anger that will come on the ungodly then, and receive the reward that will be given to the saints.

What goes on between ministers and their people is so closely and directly connected to that day. So it is especially right that these matters should be brought into that day and settled and finished there. And for this to happen, ministers and their people must meet and stand together before the great Judge on that day.

Here is how I want to use what we have seen. I want to lead you, the people here who have been in my care as your pastor, to think about some things. I also want to give you some advice that fits our situation right now. This has to do with what was recently done to separate us, ending the relationship we have had with each other. But we still expect to meet each other before the great judgment seat on the day of judgment.

At a time like this, it is surely fitting to think deeply and seriously about that future meeting of ours, which will be so solemn. Something has just been done that will most likely separate us forever, as far as our relationship as pastor and people is concerned.
How often we have met together in God’s house as pastor and people!

How often I have spoken to you! I have taught you, advised you, warned you, guided you, and fed you. I have led the sacraments among you. You were the people placed in my care, and I was responsible for your precious souls.
But most likely this will never happen again.
The prophet Jeremiah (chapter 25,

verse 3) reminds the people how long he had worked among them as God’s servant: “From the thirteenth year of Josiah son of Amon, king of Judah, up to today—this is the twenty-third year—the Lord’s word came to me. And I have spoken to you, getting up early to speak.”
I am not trying to compare myself with the prophet Jeremiah. But in this one way I can say what he said: “I have spoken God’s word to you into the twenty-third year, getting up early to speak.”
On the 15th of this past February, it had been twenty-three years since I began working in the ministry as pastor of this church and congregation.

My strength has always been weak. My body has always been sickly, and in other ways too I was not really up to such a big responsibility. Still, I have not held back my weak strength. I have used it all for the good of your souls.
I can say to you what the apostle Paul said to his listeners in Galatians 4,
verse 13: “You know that I preached the gospel to you while my body was weak.”
I have spent the best years of my life and my strength working for your eternal good.

You are my witnesses. Whatever strength I have had, I have not wasted in laziness. I have not used it to chase worldly plans or run business affairs, to get richer or to make myself and my family more important. Instead, I have given myself completely to the work of the ministry. I have worked at it night and day. I have gotten up early and put myself into this great work that Christ gave me.
I have found the work of ministry among you to be a great work indeed. It took a huge amount of care, labor, and effort. I have carried many heavy burdens in it, far too heavy for my strength.

God called me to carry these burdens. I praise his name that he has held me up so that I did not sink under them. His power has been shown in my weakness. So even though I have often been troubled on every side, I have not been overcome. I have been puzzled, but not without hope. I have been thrown down, but not destroyed.
But now I have reason to think that my work as your minister is finished. You have publicly rejected me, and my chances to serve you have come to an end.
So how important it is for us now to think about the time when we must meet each other before the chief Shepherd!

At that time I will have to give an account of how I handled the work God trusted me with. I will have to tell about the service I did for the people he sent me to, and how they received and treated me. And you will have to give an account of how you behaved toward me. You will have to tell what good you got out of these twenty-three years of my ministry.

For then you and I must both stand there together, and we both must give an account. Then a sentence will be passed on us that is perfect, right, and eternal. It will come from the one who will judge us for everything we have said or done in our meetings here. He will judge how we have treated each other, in God’s house and elsewhere, on the Sabbath and on other days. He will test our hearts and bring our thoughts into the open, along with the motives and attitudes of our minds. He will judge us, with complete fairness, on all the disagreements we have had. And he will examine how we treated each other in those disagreements.

Nothing is covered up that will not be uncovered, and nothing is hidden that will not be known. Everything will be examined in the searching, piercing light of God’s glory and of his knowledge of all things. It will be examined by the one whose eyes are like a flame of fire. Truth and right will be shown plainly, with every veil pulled away. All error, lies, wrongdoing, and harm will be laid open, with every disguise stripped off. Every excuse that only looks good, every petty objection, and all false reasoning will vanish in a moment. None of it will be able to stand the light of that day.
Then our hearts will be turned inside out. Their secrets will be seen more plainly than our outward actions are seen now.
Then it will be clear what goals we were aiming at. It will be clear what principles guided what we did. And it will be clear what attitudes we showed in our church arguments and struggles.

Then it will be clear whether I acted honestly in some earlier church disputes. It will show whether I acted out of a truly sincere and careful concern for my duty to my great Lord and Master. Those disputes led to very unhappy situations and results. It will become clear whether there was any good reason for the anger people showed at those times.

And then our recent great dispute will be examined and judged in every part and detail. That dispute was about what a person needs in order to be admitted as a full member of the visible church of Christ, with all its privileges. The whole matter will be shown in a clear, certain, and perfect light.

Then it will be clear whether what I have preached and published about this matter is Christ’s own teaching. It will be clear whether he will claim it as one of the precious truths that came from his own mouth. It will show whether he will defend it and honor it as his before the whole universe.
Then it will be clear what is meant by “the man who comes without the wedding clothes.” For that is the day spoken of in Matthew 22,
verse 13. On that day such a person will be tied up hand and foot and thrown into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and grinding of teeth.

And then it will be clear what moved me in teaching this doctrine, in acting on it, and in the way I handled the whole matter. Was I moved by my own earthly interests or honor? Did I want to look wiser than others? Did I act from any hidden, selfish, worldly motives at all? Or did I act out of a careful, strict, and tender concern for the will of my Lord and Master? Was it because I did not dare to offend him, once I was sure what his will was? I became sure of it only after a long, careful, fair, and prayerful search. All that time I kept one thing in mind, and it made me very careful not to decide too quickly that the truth was on this side of the question, where I am now convinced it is. I knew that such a decision would not help my earthly interests. It would work against them in every way. It would bring me a long chain of terrible difficulties and throw me into a deep pit of trouble and sorrow.

And then it will be clear whether my people have done their duty to their pastor in this matter. It will show whether they have had the right attitude and spirit at this time. It will show whether they were fair to me. Did they listen to, pay attention to, and think about the evidence I gave for what I believed and taught as part of God’s message? It will show whether I was treated with the fairness, openness, and respect that the just Judge thought I deserved. It will show whether goodness, love, and Christian good manners were kept up in the many steps taken and the many things said and done during this dispute. Or, if not, it will show how badly these things were broken.

Then every step each of us took in this matter, from beginning to end, will be examined and shown. So will the spirit we showed in all of it. Our own consciences will speak plainly and loudly. Each of us will be convinced, and the world will know. And for all eternity there will never again be any mistake, false report, or misunderstanding about the matter.

As far as this world goes, this dispute between you and me has probably now come to an end. It ended with what happened the week before last. But it must be decided again on that great day, which will surely come, when you and I will meet together before the great judgment seat. So I leave it until then, and I will say no more about it for now.
But now I want to speak directly to several groups of people.
I. First, to those among us who claim to be godly.
I now call you to think seriously about that great day. On that day you must meet the man who used to be your pastor, before the Judge whose eyes are like a flame of fire.

I have tried as hard as I could to search the word of God for the signs that mark true faith. These are the signs by which people can best find out their true condition and judge themselves most surely and clearly.

From time to time I have applied these rules and signs to you in my preaching. I did it with all the skill I had, and in the plainest and most searching way I could. I wanted to expose the hypocrite who is fooling himself. And I wanted to make the hopes and comforts of sincere believers firm.

And yet I am afraid that, after all I have done, I am now leaving some of you fooled and deceived. For among several hundred people who claim to be Christians, we cannot suppose that none are deceived.
From now on I will probably have no more chance to take care of your souls, or to examine and search them.

But I still beg you to remember and think about the rules I have often given you during my ministry. Think about them with that future day seriously in mind, when you and I must meet together before our Judge. On that day the calls to test yourselves that you heard from me will be repeated before you. Those rules for testing will themselves be tested, and it will be clear whether they were good or not. It will also be clear whether you listened to them fairly and tested yourselves by them. The Judge himself, who never makes mistakes, will test both you and me. After that, no one will be fooled about the state of their soul.

I have often reminded you of this: whatever you have claimed about your experiences, insights, comforts, and joys, on that day everyone will be judged by what he has done. And then you will find out that it is true.

I pray that you will get a minister who knows the word of God better than I do. May he understand the needs of souls better and be more skilled at speaking to people’s hearts. May his sermons search you more deeply and convince you more. Then those of you who have held on to a lie under my preaching may have your eyes opened by his. May you see the truth before that great day.

We do not know what help you will have in the future for learning and for examining yourselves. But one thing is certain. Time is short. Your chance to fix mistakes in such an important matter will soon be over.
We live in a world of great changes.

A great change has happened now. You have left my ministry, after sitting under it for so many years. But the time is coming, and coming soon, when you will pass out of time into eternity. Then you will be beyond the reach of every way God offers his grace.

Most of you who claim to be godly have, in the apostle’s words, “acknowledged me in part.” Until now you have accepted me as your spiritual father. You have seen me as the one God used to bring you the greatest good any human being can ever receive.

Think about that day when you and I will meet before our Judge. Then it will be examined whether I treated you the way spiritual children should be treated. And it will be examined whether you treated me the way you should have treated a spiritual father.

In God’s eyes, children owe a great deal to their natural parents. In many ways, people owe even more to a spiritual father, when they believe God used him to bring about their conversion and eternal salvation. See 1 Corinthians 4,
verse 15: “For even if you have ten thousand teachers in Christ, you do not have many fathers. For in Christ Jesus I have fathered you through the gospel.”

II. Now that I am saying goodbye to this people, I want to speak to those among them whom I am leaving without Christ and without grace. I call on them to think seriously about that solemn day when they and I must meet before the Judge of the world.

In some ways, my parting from you is an especially sad one, because I am leaving you in a very sad condition. I am leaving you in the bitterness and chains of sin. God’s anger is resting on you. You are still condemned to everlasting misery and destruction.

Since I have to leave you, it would have made our parting comforting and happy if I were leaving you in Christ. Then you would be safe and blessed in that sure shelter and glorious rest of God’s people.
But that is not how it is.

I am leaving you far away from God, as outsiders and strangers. You are miserable slaves and captives of sin and Satan. You are prisoners waiting for God’s punishing justice. You are without Christ and without God in the world.
Your own consciences know that while I had the chance, I never stopped warning you and showing you your danger.
I have worked hard to describe your misery and your great need as clearly as possible.

I have tried every way I could think of to wake up your consciences. I wanted you to see that you must use your time well. I wanted you to hurry to escape from the coming wrath, and to be thorough in using every means to escape and be safe.
I have worked hard to find and use the strongest reasons to persuade you to care about your own well-being and salvation.

I have not only tried to wake you up so that you would be moved by fear. I have also done everything I could to win you over. I have looked for pleasing words, so that, if possible, I could persuade you to leave sin behind, turn to God, and accept Christ as your Savior and Lord.
I have used up a great deal of my strength on these things.
But with you, the ones I am speaking to now, I have not succeeded. Today I have reason to complain in the words of Jeremiah 6,

verse 29: “The bellows are burned up, and the lead is used up by the fire. The metalworker melts the metal for nothing, because the wicked are not removed.” I am afraid that, for many of you, all my work has only made you harder. The word I preached was meant to be a sweet smell that brings life. But I fear that for you it has been a smell of death that leads to death.

From now on I will not have to give an account for those who have openly and firmly rejected my ministry, as if they were still placed in my care. But remember this: you must give an account for yourselves. You will have to answer for how you cared for your own souls. You will have to answer for how you used every help God gave you, past and future, through your whole lives.
Only God knows what will happen to your poor souls, which are perishing. Only he knows what help you will have from now on, or what setbacks and temptations you will face.

May God in his mercy grant this: even though all the help you have had in the past has failed, may you have new help in the future that will work in a new way. And may the word of God, as it is preached to you from now on, be like the fire and the hammer that smashes the rock to pieces.
But now, as I leave, let me urge you and beg you not to forget completely the warnings you heard while I was your minister.
When you and I meet on the day of judgment, you will remember them. Seeing me, your former minister, on that day will quickly bring them back to your mind, and in a very moving way.
Oh, don’t let that be the first time they come back to you like that!
You and I are now parting from each other as far as this world goes. Let’s work hard so that we will not be parted after we meet on the last day.
If I have been a faithful pastor to you (and that day will show whether I have or not), then I will be declared innocent, and I will go up with Christ.
Oh, do your part, so that you will not then be forced to be separated forever from me and from all who have been faithful in Christ Jesus!
This parting between you and me now is a sad one. But that parting would be much sadder for you than this one.
You may be able to handle this parting without feeling it very much, if you are not actually glad about it. But a parting like that on that day will hurt you deeply, sharply, and terribly.
III. Next, I want to speak to those who have begun to be awakened to their need.

Praise God that there are some like this. I have reason to fear that I am leaving many, many people in this large congregation without Christ. Still, I am not leaving all of them completely numb and careless about their souls.
Some of you who I hope are being awakened have told me about your situation. That makes me feel a special concern for you as I say goodbye.
I do not know how your present struggles of mind will turn out. But it will be known on that day when you and I meet before the judgment seat of Christ.
So think a lot about that day now.

Now that I am leaving this flock, I want to press on you once more the advice I have given before. Be careful not to treat such a great matter lightly. Be thorough and truly serious about it. Watch out that you do not slide back. Hold on, and keep going to the end.
And cry out strongly to God, so that the great changes happening in this church and congregation do not ruin you.
These changes bring great temptation. The devil will surely try to use them to his advantage. If he can, he will make your present convictions and efforts come to nothing.
You need to work twice as hard. Watch and pray, so that temptation does not defeat you.

Whoever becomes your spiritual guide from now on, this is my wish and prayer for you. I pray that the great Shepherd of the sheep will pay special attention to you and be your guide, for no one teaches like him. I pray that he, the endless fountain of light, will “open your eyes and turn you from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan to God, so that you may receive forgiveness of sins and an inheritance among those who are made holy through faith that is in Christ.” Then, on that great day, when I meet you again before your Judge and mine, we may meet in joy and glory, never to be separated again.
IV. Now I want to speak to the young people of the congregation.

Ever since I became the minister here, I have had a special concern for the souls of the young people. I have wanted faith to grow strong among them, and I have worked especially hard for that. I did this because I knew they had a special opportunity that others did not have. I also knew that, usually, those whom God planned to show mercy to were brought to fear and love him while they were young.
It has always seemed to me an especially lovely thing to see young people living in goodness and Christian devotion, with their hearts made pure and sweet by God’s love at work in them.

It has seemed to me a very beautiful thing, and something that would make the town better and happier, if the young people could be persuaded to act like Christians and children of God when they get together. They would stay away from impurity, silliness, and wild behavior. They would stick closely to what is right, and they would talk together about God and Christ and heaven.
This is what I have longed for. And it has hurt me deeply when I have heard about sin, empty living, and disorder among our young people.
As far as I know my own heart, this is why I once led this church to take some steps to stop sin among our young people. Those steps offended many people very much, and they made me greatly disliked.
I have wanted what is good for our young people, not what would hurt them.

I have wanted them to have true honor and happiness, not shame. I knew that true goodness and faith lead not only to glory and joy for young people in the next world, but also to their greatest peace and success and their highest dignity and honor in this world. Above all, I knew they make even the days of youth sweet, pleasant, and delightful.

Whether I have loved you and wanted your good more or less, God in his plan is now calling me to leave you. I am handing your souls over to him, the one who once gave me the job of caring for them as your pastor. So, as I say goodbye, only one thing is left for me to do. I earnestly beg you, out of love for yourselves if you have no love for me, not to look down on or forget the warnings and advice I have given you so often. Remember the day when you and I must meet again before the great Judge of the living and the dead. On that day it will be clear whether what I taught you was true and whether my advice was good. It will be clear whether I truly wanted your good, and whether you made good use of my efforts.
From time to time I have strongly warned you against “frolicking,” as people call it, and against some other freedoms that young people in this land often take.

Some people may defend these freedoms and customs, and some may laugh at warnings against them. But whatever they say, I now leave you my final warning against such things. I have no doubt that God will approve it and confirm it on that day when we meet before him.
V. Now I want to speak to the children of the congregation, the lambs of this flock, who have been in my care for so long.
I just said that I have had a special concern for the young people. When I said that, I did not mean to leave you out.

You are young, in fact the youngest of all. So I have known that if young people had a precious chance to do good for their souls, you who are very young had, in many ways, an even more precious chance.
So I have not neglected you. I have tried to be a faithful shepherd, feeding the lambs as well as the sheep.

Christ once gave me, as your minister, the care of your souls. And you know, dear children, how I have taught you and warned you from time to time. You know how I have often called you together for that purpose. And at times some of you seemed to be moved by what I told you.

But I am afraid that for many of you it has not led to salvation. I am afraid you are still not converted. God has not yet done a real saving work in your souls. Such a work would fully convince you of your sin and misery. It would make you see how terrible sin is, so that you are sorry for it and hate it more than anything. It would show you how wonderful the Lord Jesus Christ is, and bring you to hold on to him with all your heart as your Savior. It would pull your hearts away from the world. It would make you love God above everything, and enjoy holiness more than all the pleasant things of this earth. So I am afraid that I am now leaving you in a miserable condition. You have no share in Christ. You are under God’s terrible displeasure and anger, and in danger of going down into the pit of eternal misery.
But now I must say goodbye to you. I must leave you in God’s hands. I can do nothing more for you except pray for you.
I only ask you not to forget. Think often about the advice and warnings I have given you, and about the efforts I made so that your souls might be saved from everlasting destruction.
Dear children, I am leaving you in an evil world, full of traps and temptations.
Only God knows what will happen to you.
The Scripture has told us that only a few are saved. And what we see around us gives plenty of proof of this.

We see that children die as well as older people. Very many die before they grow up. And of those who do grow up, only a few, compared to the rest, ever show clear signs that they have truly been turned to God and saved.

I pray that God will have pity on you, take care of you, and give you the best help for the good of your souls. I pray that God himself will take charge of you, and be your heavenly Father and the mighty Redeemer of your souls, which will live forever.
Do not forget to pray for yourselves. Be careful that you are not one of those who throw off the fear of God and hold back their prayers from him.

Pray to God all the time in private. And often remember that great day when you must stand before the judgment seat of Christ. There you will meet your minister, who has so often advised and warned you.
I will finish with a few words of advice for everyone. They are about some things that matter very much for the well-being and success of this church and congregation.
1. If you want to be a happy people, one thing that matters greatly is keeping order in your families.

We have had big arguments about how the church should be run. And the subject of these arguments really was very important. But running your families well is just as important, and in some ways much more important.
Every Christian family should be like a little church. It should be given over to Christ and completely shaped and ruled by his rules.
Teaching and order in the family are among the most important ways God gives his grace.
If these fail, all the other ways are likely to do no good.
If these are kept up properly, all the means of grace are likely to do well and succeed.

So, before I stop speaking to this congregation for good, let me say once more the advice I have often pressed on the heads of families here while I was their pastor. Take great care in teaching, warning, and guiding your children. Bring them up in the training and correction of the Lord. Start early, while there is still a chance, and keep working at this steadily. Remember that if you do not want all your teaching and advice to be wasted, you must have discipline as well as teaching. You must keep it up fairly and firmly. It protects the faith and morals of the family and holds up its good order.
Be careful that none of you is like Eli long ago, who scolded his sons but did not stop them. Be careful that you do not bring the same kind of curse on your families that he brought on his.
And let children obey their parents, follow their teaching, and do what they tell them, if they want to receive a blessing and not a curse.

For many things in the word of God give us reason to think this: nothing is more likely to bring a curse on people in this world, and on all their earthly affairs, than children who are disobedient, stubborn, and unruly toward their parents.
2. If you want this community to do well in the future, it is extremely important that you avoid quarreling.
A quarrelsome people will be a miserable people.

The quarrels among you since I first became your pastor have been one of the heaviest burdens I have carried in my ministry. I mean not only the quarrels you have had with me, but also those you have had with one another about your land and other matters. They were a burden because I knew that quarreling, hot tempers, speaking evil, and things like that are the exact opposite of the spirit of Christianity. I knew they are especially likely to drive God’s Spirit away from a people and make all the means of grace useless. They also destroy a people’s outward comfort and well-being.
So let me strongly urge you, if you want your own good in the future, to guard against a quarrelsome spirit.
If you want to see good days, look for peace and go after it. See 1 Peter 3,
verses 10 and 11. The recent quarrel about who may be admitted to Christian communion has been the biggest of your quarrels. Let it also be the last.
Now that I am preaching my farewell sermon, I want to say to you what the apostle said to the Corinthians in 2 Corinthians 13,
verses 11 and 12: “Finally, brothers, farewell.
Be perfect. Be of one mind. Live in peace. And the God of love and peace will be with you.”
And here I especially want to advise those who stood with me in the recent dispute. Watch over your attitudes, and avoid all bitterness toward others.
In some ways your temptations are the greatest, because what has happened recently is painful to you.
But however wrong you think others have been, work hard and stay alert to keep a Christian gentleness and calmness of spirit. In this, try to do better than those on the other side.
This will be the best victory. For “the one who controls his temper is better than one who captures a city.”
So do nothing out of rivalry or pride.

Do not give in to a spirit of revenge in any way. Watch and pray against it. Do everything you can to help the town do well. And never think you are acting as Christians should unless you sincerely, deeply, and warmly love all people. Love them whatever their side or opinion, whether they are friendly or unkind, fair or unfair to you or your friends, or to the cause and kingdom of Christ.

3. Another thing that matters greatly for the future of this town is that you guard against false teaching creeping in. Watch especially against Arminianism and teachings that lead in the same direction.
As I remember well, many of you were very alarmed almost sixteen years ago. You feared that these corrupt ideas might take over.
But the danger then was small compared with the danger now.

These teachings are much more widespread today than they were then. In the last seven years they seem to have spread through the land much faster than in any other period of the same length before. And they are still spreading and creeping into almost every part of the land. They threaten to completely destroy people’s trust in those doctrines that are the special glory of the gospel. They also threaten true, living faith.
And lately I have noticed some things among you that show you are far from out of danger. In fact, you are very much exposed to it.

The older people may think they are well protected against this infection. But everyone should beware of trusting themselves too much and of feeling falsely safe. Everyone should remember these needed warnings from the holy Scriptures: “Do not be proud, but be afraid,” and “Let the one who stands watch out so that he does not fall.”
But whatever is true of the older people, the younger generation is surely in great danger.
These ideas are very attractive to our sinful nature. Young people are easily led away by them, at least those whose hearts have not been made firm by grace.

These ideas have recently taken over another large town I could name. That town used to be well known for its faith, and had been for a long time. If these ideas take over this town in the same way, they will threaten the spiritual and eternal ruin of this people, now and in the generations to come.
So you need to be as careful and watchful as possible about this matter.
4. Another thing I would advise, so that you may do well in the future, is that you devote yourselves to prayer.
God is the source of every blessing and all success, and he wants people to come to him and ask for his blessing.
So I advise you to pray faithfully in private and with your families, and to be faithful in public worship in God’s house. But I also advise you to meet often in small groups for prayer.

Some of you are grieved over the troubles of God’s people and deeply moved by the troubles of this town. I advise all of you who feel this way, whatever your opinion about our recent dispute, to meet together often to pray. Cry out to God for mercy for yourselves, mercy for this town, and mercy for Zion and for God’s people everywhere in the world.

5. The last piece of advice I want to give (and it surely matters greatly for your success) is this: be very careful when you settle a new minister. Make sure you know who he is and what kind of person he is. Pay attention especially to these two things:
(1) He must be a man whose beliefs are completely sound in all the doctrine he holds.
You will need this more than anything, especially in a time as corrupt as this.
And to find such a man, you will need to be extremely careful and wise.
I know the danger.

I know how many young gentlemen with corrupt beliefs behave. I know how they hide themselves. They put on attractive disguises that look good, and by them they fool others. They do this to protect their reputation, to win people’s trust and get hired, and to make their own position safe and secure. Then, when they see a good chance, they begin to bring out and spread their corrupt teachings more openly.
(2) Work to find a man who is known for serious faith and warm devotion to God.
It is always and everywhere very important that those who serve in this work be men of true godliness. But it is even more important at certain times, and in certain towns and churches.
Now is a time when faith is in danger from so many corruptions in teaching and in living. So now, in a special way, is a time when such ministers are needed.

At a time like this, only sincere godliness of heart can be trusted to protect a young man who is just starting out from the spreading infection. Nothing else can make him fully committed to fighting well against the flood of error and prejudice. That flood rises against the high, deep gospel teachings of the religion of Jesus Christ, and against their true results in real, experienced faith.
And this place especially needs such a minister, for reasons everyone can see.

Suppose you happened to settle a minister who does not truly know Christ or the way of salvation through him. Suppose he knew nothing from experience about what living faith is. How sad! You would be left open to danger, like sheep without a shepherd!
This place needs someone who is especially fit to stand in the gap and repair the broken wall. It needs someone who will be like the chariots and horsemen of Israel.
You need someone who will stand as a champion for the truth and for the power of godliness.
I have briefly given these important pieces of advice. Now nothing is left but for me to take my leave and say goodbye to you all. I wish and pray for the very best for you.
Now I entrust your souls, which will live forever, to the one who once entrusted them to me. I look ahead to the day when I must meet you again before him, the Judge of the living and the dead.
I hope that I will never forget this people, who were in my special care for so long. And I hope that I will never stop praying warmly for your good.

May God bless you with a faithful pastor. May he know God’s mind and will well. May he warn sinners thoroughly, test those who claim to be Christians wisely and skillfully, and lead you on the way to eternal happiness.
May you truly have a burning and shining light set up in this lampstand. And may you be willing to enjoy his light, not just for a while, but for his whole life, and may it be a long life.
And I ask to be remembered in the prayers of all God’s people who have a calm spirit and are peaceful and faithful in Israel, whatever their opinion about the terms of church communion.

And let us all remember, and never forget, our solemn meeting in the future on that great day of the Lord. It will be the day of the perfect decision, and of the sentence that lasts forever and can never be changed. Amen.
